w:r.w:t: Step 2 — The object the problem asks for: Euclidean fields, the axioms of Osterwalder and Schrader, and the reconstruction theorem
DATE: 1973–1975 (Osterwalder and Schrader). STATUS: PROVED.
The mathematics

A Euclidean quantum field theory in d dimensions is given by its Schwinger functions S_n, n ≥ 1: continuous linear functionals on test functions of n points of ℝ^d. For the composite fields from which a gauge theory is built, the test functions vanish, with all their derivatives, wherever two points coincide. Let θ be the reflection x_d ↦ −x_d in the last coordinate (Euclidean time), let τ_v be the translation by v, and let 𝒮₊ consist of the test functions supported where every point has positive last coordinate. A finite family is a sequence f = (f₀, f₁, …, f_N) with f_n ∈ 𝒮₊(ℝ^{dn}); it stands for a polynomial in the smeared field, and for t ≥ 0 the correlation of the reflected, conjugated family with its translate is
S(θf̄ · τ_t f) = Σ_{n, n′} S_{n+n′}(θf̄_n ⊗ τ_t f_{n′}).

The axioms of Osterwalder and Schrader (Comm. Math. Phys. 31 (1973), 83–112; Comm. Math. Phys. 42 (1975), 281–305) are five. (E0) Regularity: each S_n is a distribution on its test space; the reconstruction theorem below uses the strengthened form (E0′) of the second paper, the linear growth condition, which bounds |S_n(f)| by one Schwartz seminorm of f of degree proportional to n with constants growing at most as a power of n!, and whose inequality is stated there in its exact form. (E1) Euclidean invariance: S_n(h·f) = S_n(f) for every Euclidean motion h of ℝ^d. (E2) Reflection positivity: S(θf̄ · f) ≥ 0 for every finite family f. (E3) Symmetry: each S_n is invariant under permutations of its arguments. (E4) Cluster property: for finite families f, g and every spatial vector v ≠ 0, S(θf̄ · τ_{sv} g) → S(θf̄) S(g) as s → ∞.

Theorem (Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction). Schwinger functions satisfying (E0) in its strengthened form and (E1)–(E3) determine a Hilbert space ℋ, a unit vector Ω, a positive self-adjoint Hamiltonian H with HΩ = 0, a unitary representation of the Poincaré group and Wightman fields, from which the S_n are recovered by analytic continuation. Each finite family f defines a vector [f] ∈ ℋ; these vectors are dense in ℋ, ⟨Ω, [f]⟩ = S(f), and for t ≥ 0
Given (E0)–(E3), the cluster property (E4) holds exactly when Ω is, up to a phase, the only vector invariant under the translations.
The explanation

Reflection positivity is the axiom that manufactures the Hilbert space. On the finite families supported at positive time the form ⟨f, g⟩ := S(θf̄ · g) is a positive semidefinite sesquilinear form by (E2); the quotient by its null vectors, completed, is ℋ, and the class of the empty family is the vacuum Ω. Translation in time by t ≥ 0 maps 𝒮₊ into itself and is a contraction for this form by (E1) and (E2) together, and the contractions e^{−tH} so obtained form a strongly continuous self-adjoint semigroup; its generator H is positive and self-adjoint, and HΩ = 0 because the empty family is fixed by every translation. Spatial translations and the remaining Euclidean motions give the unitary representation; the analytic continuation of the Schwinger functions in the time differences, which (E0) in its strengthened form guarantees, gives the Wightman functions and the Wightman fields (Glimm and Jaffe, Quantum Physics: A Functional Integral Point of View, second edition, 1987, Chapter 6). The mass gap of the conclusion is a property of exactly this H: the problem is a statement about the spectrum of the operator that reflection positivity constructs, and nothing about any other operator.
Consistency

Uses Step 1. The Hilbert space ℋ, the vacuum Ω and the Hamiltonian H named here are the ℋ, Ω and H of the conclusion's spectral condition. Every later step that constructs Schwinger functions on a lattice and passes to a limit is measured against (E0)–(E4) as stated here, and the lattice form of this theorem is Step 4.
Step 3 — Wilson's lattice gauge theory
DATE: 1974 (Wilson). STATUS: PROVED.
The mathematics

Let G be a compact Lie group, G = SU(N) in what follows, and let Λ be the periodic lattice of spacing a and side L in d = 4 dimensions. To each oriented bond b of Λ is assigned a group element U_b ∈ G with U_{−b} = U_b^{−1}, and to each plaquette p (an elementary square of the lattice, with an orientation) the ordered product U_p of the four bond variables around it. Wilson's measure (K. G. Wilson, "Confinement of quarks", Phys. Rev. D 10 (1974), 2445–2459) is
dμ_β(U) = Z^{−1} exp( −β Σ_p ( 1 − (1/N) Re tr U_p ) ) Π_b dU_b,

with dU_b the normalised Haar measure of G on each bond and Z the normalising constant. It is invariant under the gauge transformations U_{xy} ↦ g_x U_{xy} g_y^{−1}, g : Λ → G, and the observables of the theory are the gauge-invariant functions of the bond variables. For SU(2) the plaquette energy a_p(U) = 1 − ½ tr U_p ∈ [0, 2] is the gauge-invariant scalar whose smeared and centred sums are the theory's basic observable, the lattice form of the action density tr F².
The explanation

Gauge invariance is a change of variables: the Haar measure is invariant under left and right multiplication, each plaquette product transforms as U_p ↦ g_x U_p g_x^{−1} at its base point x, and the trace is a class function, so the exponent is unchanged. Because G is compact and the Haar measure is a probability measure, dμ_β is a probability measure on the compact space G^{bonds} for every β ≥ 0 with no gauge fixing: the lattice theory is a well-defined measure at every coupling, which is why the lattice is the setting of every construction that follows. With U_{x,μ} = exp(i a g A_μ(x)) for a smooth connection A and β = 2N/g², the exponent is a Riemann sum of the Yang–Mills action ¼ ∫ F^a_{μν} F^a_{μν} d⁴x as a → 0, which is the sense in which Wilson's theory is the lattice form of Yang–Mills theory. The correlations of the plaquette energy at distinct sites are Schwinger functions of a composite field, the lattice forms of the S_n of Step 2 for the field tr F².
Consistency

Uses Steps 1–2. Every lattice quantity in this document — a gap, a clustering rate, a coupling — is a quantity of this measure dμ_β or of its blocked and effective descendants, and every group G of the conclusion enters through this definition.
Step 4 — Reflection positivity, the transfer matrix and the lattice gap
DATE: 1912 (Jentzsch); 1977 (Lüscher); 1978 (Osterwalder and Seiler); the kernel form of the finite gap 2026-10-27. STATUS: PROVED.
The mathematics

Theorem (Osterwalder and Seiler, "Gauge field theories on a lattice", Ann. Physics 110 (1978), 440–471). Wilson's measure is reflection positive: if ϑ is the reflection of Λ in a lattice hyperplane orthogonal to a coordinate axis and F is a function of the bond variables on one side of it, then ∫ ϑF̄ · F dμ_β ≥ 0.

Theorem (Lüscher, "Construction of a selfadjoint, strictly positive transfer matrix for Euclidean lattice gauge theories", Comm. Math. Phys. 54 (1977), 283–292). For Wilson's action there is a self-adjoint, strictly positive transfer matrix T acting on the gauge-invariant functions of the bond variables of one time slice, such that time-ordered correlations on a torus of time extent Na are traces of products of T with the observables. On a torus of finite spatial volume T is an integral operator with a continuous, strictly positive kernel on a compact space.

Theorem (Jentzsch, "Über Integralgleichungen mit positivem Kern", J. Reine Angew. Math. 141 (1912), 235–244). An integral operator with a continuous, strictly positive kernel on a compact space has a largest eigenvalue λ₀ that is simple, with a strictly positive eigenfunction ψ₀, and every other eigenvalue is strictly smaller in modulus.
Definition (the lattice gap). Let λ₁ be the largest eigenvalue of T below λ₀ on the gauge-invariant sector. The lattice mass gap is
m_lat = log(λ₀/λ₁)

in units of the lattice spacing; its value in physical units is m_lat/a. In the state defined by ψ₀, which is the limit of infinite time extent at fixed spatial volume, an observable A of the bond variables at positive times defines, by integration over the half-lattice with A inserted, a vector Φ_A on the time slice, and for every number n of time steps
⟨ϑĀ · τ_n A⟩₀ = ⟨Φ_A, (T/λ₀)^n Φ_A⟩.

The finite form of the definition is a theorem of the Lean 4 kernel above the Mathlib library, with no unproved step: for an entrywise-positive symmetric matrix T on a finite cross-section, every eigenvalue λ_i other than the Perron root λ₀ satisfies λ₀ − |λ_i| > 0, and in energies log λ₀ − log |λ_i| > 0 whenever λ_i ≠ 0 (theorems finite_volume_mass_gap and finite_volume_mass_gap_log of the file Aperanton/MassGap.lean; the Perron root's simplicity and strict dominance for such matrices, the finite-dimensional form of Jentzsch's theorem, in Aperanton/Perron.lean, which is Perron's theorem of 1907 and Frobenius's of 1912).
The explanation

Reflection positivity makes the lattice theory a quantum mechanics: it is the lattice form of axiom (E2), and the construction of Step 2 applied to it gives the Hilbert space of gauge-invariant functions of one time slice on which T acts, with T/λ₀ playing the part of e^{−aH} for one unit of Euclidean time. The problem statement calls this positivity "a major advantage" and adds that "establishing a quantum mechanical Hilbert space is part of the solution to this Millennium problem" (Jaffe and Witten, the official problem description, §6.5). Jentzsch's theorem is what makes the vacuum unique on every finite spatial volume at every coupling: the kernel of T is a product of Boltzmann factors of a bounded action, hence strictly positive and continuous on the compact group manifold of the slice's bond variables, so λ₀ is simple and every other eigenvalue is strictly smaller. The lattice gap is therefore strictly positive on every finite cross-section at every coupling; the content of the problem is that this gap, divided by the spacing, stays bounded below as the volume grows and the spacing shrinks along the sequence of couplings fixed by asymptotic freedom.
Consistency

Uses Steps 1–3. The identity ⟨ϑĀ · τ_n A⟩₀ = ⟨Φ_A, (T/λ₀)^n Φ_A⟩ is the lattice form of Step 2's ⟨[f], e^{−tH}[f]⟩ = S(θf̄ · τ_t f). The gap m_lat defined here is the quantity every later lattice bound concerns, and m_lat/a is what must stay bounded below for the conclusion's Δ.
Step 5 — The gap governs reflection-positive decay
DATE: 2026-10-27 (the kernel form) and 2026-10-28 (the lemma). STATUS: PROVED.
The mathematics
Lemma. Let q = λ₁/λ₀. For every gauge-invariant observable A at positive times and every n ≥ 0,
0 ≤ ⟨ϑĀ · τ_n A⟩₀ − |⟨A⟩₀|² ≤ q^n ( ⟨ϑĀ · A⟩₀ − |⟨A⟩₀|² ).

Proof. Write Φ_A = ⟨ψ₀, Φ_A⟩ψ₀ + φ with φ ⊥ ψ₀. Since ⟨ψ₀, Φ_A⟩ = ⟨A⟩₀ and ψ₀ is fixed by T/λ₀, the middle term equals ⟨φ, (T/λ₀)^n φ⟩. The operator T/λ₀ is positive, and on the orthogonal complement of ψ₀ its norm is q. Hence 0 ≤ ⟨φ, (T/λ₀)^n φ⟩ ≤ q^n ‖φ‖², and ‖φ‖² = ⟨ϑĀ · A⟩₀ − |⟨A⟩₀|² is the case n = 0. ∎

The finite form of the lemma is a theorem of the Lean 4 kernel above the Mathlib library, with no unproved step (theorem twopoint_le_of_gap of the file Aperanton/Scaling.lean): for a positive semidefinite matrix M with strictly positive entries, a number q ≥ 0 such that every eigenvalue other than the Perron root λ₀ is at most q λ₀, any real vector f and any R ≥ 0, there is a Perron eigenvector Ω of M with every entry nonzero such that
0 ≤ f · (M^R f) / λ₀^R − (Ω · f)² ≤ (f · f) q^R.

Its proof in the kernel is the moment representation: f · (M^R f) = Σ_k m_k λ_k^R with m_k ≥ 0 the squared components of f along an orthonormal eigenbasis, Σ_k m_k = f · f, the Perron term m_{k₀} λ₀^R = (Ω · f)² λ₀^R removed, and every other term bounded by m_k (q λ₀)^R.
The explanation

The lemma is the spectral theorem applied once: a gap in the spectrum of the transfer matrix forces every connected reflection-positive two-point function to decay at least geometrically in the time separation, at the rate q = e^{−m_lat}, and to be nonnegative. Two features of the bound carry the later steps. The constant on the right, ⟨ϑĀ · A⟩₀ − |⟨A⟩₀|², is a correlation between A and its mirror image, whose supports are separated by twice the distance of A from the reflection plane; it is therefore controlled by bounds on correlations at separated points, which is the only kind of bound a construction of a composite field can provide. And on a torus of finite time extent N the correlations differ from those of the state ψ₀ by terms bounded, at a fixed lattice, by multiples of q^{N−n} and of tr(T/λ₀)^N − 1, which tend to zero as the time extent grows at fixed spatial volume; the kernel's theorem mass_gap_rate of the same development gives the residual bound |tr(T^L) − λ₀^L| ≤ (dim − 1)(ρλ₀)^L with ρ < 1 that controls the second term.
Consistency

Uses Steps 1–4; q is Step 4's λ₁/λ₀ and ψ₀, Φ_A are Step 4's. The inequality is used, in the direction gap ⇒ decay, by every later step that turns a lattice gap into exponential clustering, and its converse, decay ⇒ gap, is the content of the equivalence proved later for reflection-positive theories.
